lesson.title: Settling Down at the Edges: Horizontal Asymptotes
lesson.summary: A horizontal asymptote describes the finite value a function's output settles toward as the input grows without bound in either direction, and for rational functions it can be read directly from the degrees of the numerator and denominator.
lesson.body:
A horizontal asymptote is the long-run counterpart to a vertical asymptote. The line y = L is a horizontal asymptote of f if the limit of f(x) as x approaches positive infinity equals L, or the limit as x approaches negative infinity equals L. Because these are two separate, independent conditions, a single function can approach two different horizontal asymptotes, one on the right and a different one on the left. Unlike a vertical asymptote, which describes what happens near one fixed input value, a horizontal asymptote describes what happens as the input itself grows without bound.

For a rational function f(x) = p(x)/q(x), the horizontal asymptote can be read directly from the degrees of the numerator and denominator. If the degree of p is less than the degree of q, the horizontal asymptote is y = 0, because dividing every term by the highest power in the denominator sends the entire numerator toward 0 while the denominator approaches a nonzero constant. If the degrees are equal, the horizontal asymptote is y equal to the ratio of the leading coefficients of p and q, since every lower-degree term becomes negligible in comparison. If the degree of p exceeds the degree of q, there is no horizontal asymptote at all, since the function grows without bound instead of leveling off, a case picked up by the oblique asymptote discussion next.

For a worked example, take f(x) = (2x^2 + 3)/(x^2 - 1). Both numerator and denominator have degree 2, so divide every term by x^2, the highest power present: f(x) = (2 + 3/x^2)/(1 - 1/x^2). As x approaches infinity, both 3/x^2 and 1/x^2 approach 0, so f(x) approaches (2 + 0)/(1 - 0) = 2. The same computation holds as x approaches negative infinity, since 3/x^2 and 1/x^2 approach 0 regardless of the sign of x. So y = 2 is a horizontal asymptote in both directions.

A quick numerical check confirms the algebra: at x = 100, f(100) = (2(10000) + 3)/(10000 - 1) = 20003/9999, which is approximately 2.0005, very close to 2 and closing in as x grows larger. For comparison, a case with unequal degrees is g(x) = 5/(x - 1); here the numerator has degree 0 and the denominator has degree 1, so as x approaches infinity the fraction shrinks toward 0, giving a horizontal asymptote of y = 0 even though the function never actually reaches that value for any finite x.

Horizontal asymptotes describe the eventual leveling height of a graph but say nothing about behavior near specific finite inputs, which is the job of vertical asymptotes instead. A single function can have both: the example above also has vertical asymptotes at x = 1 and x = -1, since the denominator x^2 - 1 vanishes at those points while the numerator, evaluating to 5 and 5 respectively, does not. The degree-comparison shortcut used here is really just a convenient way to compute a limit at infinity, the formal topic taken up in the next section, where the same reasoning is stated as a general rule rather than a memorized set of cases.
